d.title: Comma-separated is a convention, not a rule
d.caption: A European export uses semicolons because the decimal separator is a comma; a log export uses tabs or pipes. And a field that contains the delimiter must be quoted — which is where malformed files come from, because the writer that forgot to quote it produced a file with the wrong number of columns on one row.

d.title: The pattern of garbage identifies the mismatch
d.caption: Mojibake is not random: each wrong pairing produces a signature. `café` written as UTF-8 and read as Latin-1 shows `cafÃ©`, because the two bytes of é are each shown as one Latin-1 character. Reading the signature tells you which encoding to pass.

d.title: A nested object becomes columns; a nested array becomes rows
d.caption: The distinction decides the **grain** of your frame. An object has fixed keys, so it flattens sideways into dotted column names. An array has no fixed length, so it can only unroll downwards — one row per element, with the parent's fields repeated on each, which is a fan-out exactly like a join.

d.title: Every JSON feed drifts, and most drift is silent
d.caption: `json_normalize` fills a missing key with NaN, which is reasonable. Everything else it handles by handing you an `object` column and no warning — so a field that changed from a string to a number still parses, and only fails three steps later when something does arithmetic on it.

d.title: How a filter skips most of the file without reading it
d.caption: A Parquet file is divided horizontally into row groups, and each row group records the min and max of every column. The reader compares the filter against those statistics before touching the data — so a query on a date range reads only the row groups whose range overlaps it. Sorting the file by the column you filter on is what makes this effective.

d.title: The row count a join produces
d.caption: The same arithmetic as a pandas merge, and the same incident: a key that appears twice on the left and three times on the right contributes six rows, and the revenue total is then triple what it should be. Predict the count before you run the query.

d.title: GROUP BY collapses; OVER does not
d.caption: They compute the same statistic. `OVER` leaves every row in place with its group's value attached, which is why it is the SQL equivalent of `groupby().transform()` — and the tool for every 'compared to its group' feature.

d.title: Results that do not fit in memory
d.caption: The default `read_sql` builds the whole result as one frame, which is fine until the day the query returns ten million rows and the process dies. Each of these moves the boundary somewhere else; the last one moves the work instead of the rows.

d.title: The checks a broken export fails and a descriptive summary passes
d.caption: Everything before this step **describes** the data. These test it. Each one is a fact that must be true if the export is intact, and a truncated or double-loaded file passes every histogram while failing these.

d.title: Correlation is undefined for two categorical columns
d.caption: There is no order to correlate. The tools are a contingency table, a chi-square test for whether the association is real, Cramér's V for how strong it is on a 0–1 scale, and mutual information for the general case that handles every combination of types.

d.title: Six dimensions, and the one that cannot be tested from the data
d.caption: Five of these are assertions you can write against the frame in front of you. Accuracy is not: asking whether a value matches reality needs something outside the dataset — a reconciliation total, a sampled audit, a second source. A pipeline that checks only the first five can be green on data that is entirely wrong.

d.title: Which failures should stop the pipeline
d.caption: A duplicated primary key will corrupt every join downstream. A 0.3% rate of malformed emails will not. The gate needs both kinds of check, and which is which is a business decision — recorded in code, so it can be argued with.

d.title: Three kinds of duplicate, and only the first is cheap
d.caption: They need different tools because they are different problems. The third cannot be found in the data at all: a maiden name and a married name are the same person and nothing about the two rows says so without a domain rule or a second identifier.

d.title: Why blocking is what makes matching possible
d.caption: Comparing every pair is n²: a hundred thousand records is five billion comparisons. Blocking only compares pairs that share a cheap key, which removes almost all of them — at the cost of missing a true pair whose block key differs, which is why the key is chosen to be the field least likely to be wrong.

d.title: What to do, by mechanism
d.caption: The mechanism decides whether a fill is honest. Under MCAR the observed rows are a fair sample, so dropping them loses power but not correctness. Under MNAR the missingness itself carries the information — and an imputed value hides exactly the thing you needed to model.

d.title: The indicator keeps the gap visible
d.caption: Any fill makes a value up. Adding a boolean column that records *where* the fill happened costs one column and lets the model use the fact of absence as a feature — which, under MNAR, is often the strongest signal in the dataset.

d.title: Why the z-score hides the outlier it is looking for
d.caption: Both μ and σ are computed from data that includes the outlier. A large value inflates σ and pulls μ towards itself, so its own z-score comes out smaller than it should — and two large outliers can hide each other completely. The quartile-based rules have no such problem because quartiles do not move.

d.title: Normal on every column, impossible as a combination
d.caption: Height 180 cm is normal. Weight 45 kg is normal. Together they describe someone who does not exist. No univariate rule sees it, because each column was checked on its own — which is the whole argument for a multivariate check.

d.title: Unusual is not wrong
d.caption: The treatment follows from which of these a row is, and that question cannot be answered by a rule on the value. An influential point is a fourth, orthogonal thing: a row can be extreme without changing the fit, or moderate and highly influential.
